title: The Engle-Granger test
objectives: Test a pair for cointegration with the two-step method.
Explain why a residual needs its own critical values.

screens.title: Test the residual
screens.prose: Lesson 1's walks A and B, seed 103, were drawn independently. Regress B on A and keep the residual, shown here. The ARMA course's ADF test on it gives a statistic of −2.91 and $p = 0.045$. Its 5% critical value is −2.86.
screens.question: Read by the ARMA course's rule, what does the test say?

options.text: It rejects a unit root, so the residual looks stationary and A and B look cointegrated
It fails to reject a unit root
options.why: −2.91 is below −2.86 and $p = 0.045$ is below 0.05. By the ADF rule, it rejects.

options.text: The ADF test cannot be run on a residual
options.why: It can be run on any series, and statsmodels runs it without complaint. The question is how to read it.

hints.text: Compare the statistic with the critical value.
Reject when the statistic is below the critical value, or $p < 0.05$.
−2.91 < −2.86 and 0.045 < 0.05: the rule says reject.

feedback.correct: Correct, by that rule. Yet A and B are independent walks, so the rule has misled us.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply the ADF rule exactly as the ARMA course did.

explain.text: By the usual ADF rule the residual is stationary, so two unrelated walks would count as cointegrated. They are not: seed 103 is two independent walks. Something about testing a residual changes the rules, and this lesson finds what.

screens.title: What unrelated pairs give
screens.prose: Seeds 0 to 999 each give two independent walks of 500 days. Regress one on the other and run the ADF test on the residual. The bars count the 1,000 statistics. None of these pairs is cointegrated.

derive.caption: {{fixed(values.beyondShare * 100, 1)}}% of the 1,000 unrelated pairs lie left of the cut

screens.question: Slide the cut until 5% of the pairs lie left of it.

hints.text: Watch the caption as you move the cut.
At −2.86, the ADF value, far more than 5% lie to the left.
The share reaches 5.0% near −3.35.

feedback.correct: That's it. 5% of unrelated pairs fall below about −3.35, not −2.86.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move the cut until the caption reads close to 5%.

byKey.adf: Near the ADF value about 15% of these unrelated pairs lie left of the cut. That is three times too many.

explain.text: 5.0% of the statistics lie below −3.35, and 14.6% below the ADF value −2.86. Seed 103's −2.91 sits among the left 12.9%: ordinary for two unrelated walks. A residual needs its own, more negative, critical values.

screens.title: The Engle-Granger test
screens.prose: Engle and Granger (1987) test a pair in two steps. Regress $y$ on $x$, then test the residual for a unit root. MacKinnon's tables give the residual's critical values. For two series with a constant and 500 days: −3.90 at 1%, −3.34 at 5%, −3.04 at 10%.
screens.question: Against the Engle-Granger 5% value, what is the verdict on A and B?

options.text: Fail to reject: −2.91 is above −3.34, so there is no evidence of cointegration
Reject: −2.91 is below −2.86
options.why: You used the ADF critical value. The residual test needs the Engle-Granger value, −3.34.

options.text: Reject at 10%, since −2.91 is close to −3.04
options.why: Close is not beyond. −2.91 is above −3.04, so even the 10% test fails to reject.

hints.text: Which point is the Engle-Granger 5% value?
Reject only if the statistic is left of −3.34.
−2.91 lies right of −3.34: fail to reject.

feedback.correct: Correct. With the right critical value, the unrelated walks are not cointegrated.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare −2.91 with the Engle-Granger value, not the ADF one.

byKey.rej: You compared with −2.86, the ADF value for a series you did not fit. A residual needs −3.34.

explain.text: OLS chose $\hat\beta$ to make the residual as small and steady as it could, so the critical values move left. statsmodels' `coint(y, x)` does both steps: statistic −2.9091, $p = 0.1334$ for A and B.

screens.title: Step one on a real tie
screens.prose: Now pair C, `make_pair(3, 1000)`, built with $\beta = 1.5$ and $\alpha = 5$. Step one, least squares of $y$ on $x$, gives $\hat\beta = 1.4744$ and $\hat\alpha = 6.4908$. On day 500, $x = £46.96$ and $y = £76.81$.
screens.question: What is the residual $\hat u = y - \hat\alpha - \hat\beta x$ on day 500? Give 2 decimal places, in pounds.

hints.text: Multiply $\hat\beta$ by $x$ first.

feedback.correct: Correct. £1.08 above the fitted line on day 500.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract both $\hat\alpha$ and $\hat\beta x$ from $y$.

byKey.true: You used the true 1.5 and 5. Step one uses the fitted $\hat\beta$ and $\hat\alpha$.

explain.text: $1.4744 \times 46.96 = 69.24$, and $76.81 - 6.49 - 69.24 = 1.08$. The residual series has sd £1.59 over the 1,000 days. Step two tests whether that series is stationary.

screens.title: Step two on a real tie
screens.prose: Step two on pair C's residual: the ADF statistic with no lags and no constant is −5.1315.
screens.question: At which levels does the Engle-Granger test reject?

options.text: At 5% and 10% only
options.why: −5.13 is left of −3.90 as well, so it rejects at 1% too.

options.text: At none: −5.13 is far from the ADF value
options.why: Far left of every critical value means reject, not the opposite.

hints.text: Which critical values lie right of −5.13?
All three Engle-Granger points are right of −5.13.
−5.13 < −3.90 < −3.34 < −3.04: it rejects at every level.

feedback.correct: Correct. Pair C is cointegrated at every usual level.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Reject wherever the statistic is left of the critical value.

explain.text: `coint(y, x)` agrees: statistic −5.1315, $p = 0.0001$. It chose the residual's lags by AIC, and AIC chose none here. It also leaves out the ADF constant, because an OLS residual already has mean zero.

screens.title: Both steps in code
screens.prose: Step one is least squares in NumPy, given. For step two, call `adfuller(res, maxlag=0, regression="n", autolag=None)`: no lags, and no constant, since the residual already has mean zero. Index 0 is the statistic.
screens.question: Complete `engle_granger_by_hand(y, x)`.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_two_walks(seed, n=500):
    """Two independent Gaussian random walks from 0 (columns of one draw)."""
    z = np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal((n, 2))
    return np.cumsum(z[:, 0]), np.cumsum(z[:, 1])


def make_pair(seed, n=1000, alpha=5.0, beta=1.5, phi=0.95, sd_u=0.5, x0=40.0, vol=0.015):
    """A cointegrated pair of share prices in pounds. x starts at x0 and is a log random walk
    with daily sd vol; y = alpha + beta * x + u, u an AR(1) with coefficient phi and shock sd sd_u."""
    z = np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal((n, 2))
    x = x0 * np.exp(np.cumsum(vol * z[:, 0]))
    u = np.empty(n); u[0] = sd_u * z[0, 1]
    for t in range(1, n):
        u[t] = phi * u[t - 1] + sd_u * z[t, 1]
    return x, alpha + beta * x + u


def make_broken_pair(seed, n=1500, break_at=1000, sd_break=1.0, **kw):
    """make_pair, plus a random walk added to y from day break_at: the spread stops reverting."""
    x, y = make_pair(seed, n, **kw)
    z = np.random.default_rng(seed + 1000).standard_normal(n)
    return x, y + np.concatenate([np.zeros(break_at), np.cumsum(sd_break * z[break_at:])])


def make_case(name, n=1000):
    """Lesson 2's four planted pairs, as (x, y)."""
    if name == "A":    # correlated returns, not cointegrated
        e = np.random.default_rng(1).standard_normal((n, 2))
        return np.cumsum(e[:, 0]), np.cumsum(0.8 * e[:, 0] + 0.6 * e[:, 1])
    if name == "B":    # cointegrated, weakly correlated returns
        e = np.random.default_rng(2).standard_normal((n, 2))
        x = np.cumsum(e[:, 0])
        u = np.empty(n); u[0] = 3 * e[0, 1]
        for t in range(1, n):
            u[t] = 0.5 * u[t - 1] + 3 * e[t, 1]
        return x, x + u
    if name == "C":    # both
        return make_pair(3, n)
    return make_two_walks(4, n)    # D: neither

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller

def engle_granger_by_hand(y, x):
    """Return (beta, alpha, residual ADF statistic), each to 4 places."""
    y, x = np.asarray(y), np.asarray(x)
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
    alpha, beta = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]    # step 1: OLS
    res = y - alpha - beta * x
    stat = adfuller(res, maxlag=0, regression="n", autolag=None)[0]
    return round(float(beta), 4), round(float(alpha), 4), round(float(stat), 4)

tests.setup: from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import coint; x, y = make_pair(3, 1000)
tests.call: round(engle_granger_by_hand(y, x)[2] - coint(y, x, maxlag=0, autolag=None)[0], 4)

tests.setup: from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import coint; x, y = make_two_walks(103)
tests.call: round(engle_granger_by_hand(y, x)[2] - coint(y, x, maxlag=0, autolag=None)[0], 4)

`adfuller` returns the statistic first.
`res = y - alpha - beta * x` and `stat = adfuller(res, maxlag=0, regression="n", autolag=None)[0]`.

feedback.correct: Correct. −2.9091 for the unrelated walks and −5.1315 for pair C, matching `coint`.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Form the residual from the fitted $\alpha$ and $\beta$, then take index 0 of `adfuller`.

explain.text: Your statistic equals `coint`'s to 4 places only with `regression="n"`. With a constant, pair C's statistic would be −5.1289: close, but not the test `coint` runs. Pair B's −19.73 shows how strongly a tied gap rejects.

screens.title: Which p-value to quote
screens.prose: For pair C's residual, two numbers are on the screen. `adfuller(res)` prints $p = 0.000012$. `coint(y, x)` prints $p = 0.000094$.
screens.question: Which p-value belongs in a report on whether the pair is cointegrated?

options.text: `coint`'s 0.000094: it judges the residual against residual critical values
`adfuller`'s 0.000012: it is the smaller, so the stronger evidence
options.why: You picked the smaller p. It is smaller because it ignores that OLS fitted the residual; it overstates the evidence.

options.text: Either: both are tiny, so the choice does not matter
options.why: Here both reject, but for seed 103 they disagree: 0.045 against 0.13. The habit matters.

hints.text: Which call knows the residual came from a fitted regression?
Look at the last column.
Only `coint` uses critical values built for residuals.

feedback.correct: Correct. Never quote `adfuller`'s p-value for a residual.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which p-value uses the right null distribution?

byKey.adf: You quoted the ADF p-value for a fitted residual. It is too small by design.

explain.text: `adfuller` compares the residual with the Dickey-Fuller null for a raw series, so its p-value is too small. `coint` uses MacKinnon's null for residuals. For seed 103 the two disagree: 0.045 against 0.1334, and only `coint` is right.

screens.title: The right and the wrong decision
screens.prose: Write the decision two ways. The right one uses `coint`; the trap reads `adfuller`'s p-value on the residual. The tests then count how often each rejects for 40 pairs of independent walks.
screens.question: Complete `eg_decision(y, x, alpha)` and `wrong_decision(y, x)`.

Reject when the p-value is below `alpha`.
`stat, p, crit = coint(y, x)`, `bool(p < alpha)`, and `p = adfuller(res, autolag="AIC")[1]`.

feedback.correct: Correct. Over 40 unrelated pairs, `coint` rejects once and the trap rejects 7 times.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Unpack `coint`'s three outputs, and take index 1 of `adfuller` in the trap.

explain.text: On 40 pairs of independent walks the right test rejects once, close to the promised 5%. The trap rejects 7 times, about 18%; over 200 seeds the counts are 10 and 35. Reading `adfuller` on a residual finds ties that are not there.

screens.title: The ADF value will do
screens.prose: A colleague tests residuals with `adfuller` and its 5% critical value, −2.86, as in the ARMA course. He screens many pairs of unrelated walks, like the 1,000 in the explore.
screens.question: About what share of unrelated pairs will he call cointegrated?

options.text: About 5%, as the test's level promises
options.why: You trusted the 5% label. That level holds for a raw series, not for a residual OLS has fitted.

options.text: About 15%
About half
options.why: Most residual statistics lie right of −2.86. About one pair in seven lies left of it.

options.text: None, since unrelated walks never give stationary residuals
options.why: Seed 103 did, by his rule: −2.91 is left of −2.86.

hints.text: Recall the explore: how many of the 1,000 lay left of −2.86?
The ADF value lies right of every Engle-Granger value.
14.6% of the unrelated pairs had a statistic below −2.86.

feedback.correct: Correct. About 15% false discoveries, three times the promised 5%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the explore's share left of −2.86.

byKey.five: You took the 5% at face value. Against −2.86, 14.6% of unrelated pairs pass.

explain.text: OLS fits $\hat\beta$ to make the residual look stationary, which pushes its statistic left. Against −2.86, 14.6% of unrelated pairs pass; against −3.34, 5.0% do. Seed 103's −2.91 lies between, which is exactly where the trap bites.

screens.title: A tie that breaks
screens.prose: `make_broken_pair(3)` is pair C for 1,000 days, then a random walk is added to $y$ from day 1,000. The chart shows $y - 1.5x - 5$. `coint` on days 0 to 999 gives $p = 0.0001$; on all 1,500 days, $p = 0.99$.
screens.question: What should a desk conclude?

options.text: The pair was tied, then the tie broke; a full-sample test hides when
The pair was never cointegrated, as the full sample shows
options.why: Days 0 to 999 give $p = 0.0001$. The tie was real until day 1,000.

options.text: It is still cointegrated, since it was for two-thirds of the sample
options.why: The last 500 days wander by up to £50. A tie that has broken cannot be traded on its past.

options.text: Average the two p-values to about 0.5
options.why: p-values do not average. The question is when the tie held.

hints.text: Look at the shaded stretch.
Before day 1,000 the gap crosses 0 often; after it, it falls away.
The tie held, then broke. One full-sample test cannot show that.

feedback.correct: Correct. Level 3 watches for breaks while a pair is traded.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the gap before and after day 1,000.

byKey.never: You trusted the full-sample test alone. It mixes a tied stretch with a broken one.

explain.text: A test on the whole sample asks one question about 1,500 days, so a late break drowns the early tie. Desks therefore test on a formation window and then monitor the live spread. Lesson 11 returns to this pair.

screens.title: The two steps
screens.prose: **Engle-Granger.** Step 1: least squares, $y_t = \hat\alpha + \hat\beta x_t + \hat u_t$. Step 2: a unit-root test on $\hat u_t$, $$\Delta \hat u_t = \gamma\, \hat u_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t,$$ with $t_\gamma$ judged against MacKinnon's residual values, about −3.34 at 5%. In code: `coint(y, x)`.
screens.question: Pair C gives −5.1315 for `coint(y, x)` and −5.109 for `coint(x, y)`. What does that show?

options.text: The test depends a little on which series is regressed on which; here both reject
One of the two calls is wrong
options.why: Both are right. Each regresses a different series on the other, so the residuals differ.

options.text: Nothing, since the test is the same both ways
options.why: The two statistics differ: −5.1315 and −5.109. The direction matters a little.

feedback.correct: Correct. Lesson 5 explains why the direction matters.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Are the two regressions the same?

explain.text: Regressing $y$ on $x$ and $x$ on $y$ give different lines and residuals, so slightly different statistics. For a strong tie both reject. Lesson 5 shows why the fitted hedge ratio depends on the direction.

screens.title: In the interview
screens.prose: A quant's pipeline: filter pairs by return correlation, then run Engle-Granger at 5% on a two-year formation window. The interviewer asks: "Why can't you use the ordinary ADF critical values on the regression residual?"

state.caption: 1,000 pairs of independent 500-day walks, from the explore.

screens.question: Choose the best two-sentence answer.

options.text: OLS picks $\hat\beta$ to make the residual as stationary-looking as possible, so it rejects more easily than a raw series. Its statistic needs MacKinnon's more negative values, about −3.34 at 5%
The residual is not normally distributed, so the ADF table does not apply. Use a bootstrap instead
options.why: Normality is not the issue. The residual was fitted, which shifts the null distribution of its statistic.

options.text: The residual needs more lags than a price series. With enough lags the ADF values are fine
options.why: Lags change the regression, not the reason. A fitted residual needs its own critical values at any lag length.

options.text: You can use them; they differ only in the third decimal place
options.why: −2.86 against −3.34 is a large gap: 14.6% false passes against 5.0%.

hints.text: What did step one do to the residual?
Compare the two rows of the table.
Fitting makes the residual look stationary, so the critical values move left.

feedback.correct: Correct. State the cause, then the fix.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The answer must say why a fitted residual is different.

byKey.normal: You blamed the shape of the residual. The problem is that OLS chose it.

explain.text: Lead with the cause: OLS minimises the residual's variance, so it looks stationary even for unrelated walks. Then the fix: MacKinnon's residual critical values, which `coint` applies. Add that 2,000 such tests at 5% still give about 100 false pairs.

ideas: Engle-Granger tests a pair in two steps: regress $y$ on $x$, then test the residual for a unit root.
The residual needs MacKinnon's critical values, about −3.34 at 5%, not the ADF −2.86: OLS made it look stationary. `coint(y, x)` does both steps.
A full-sample test can hide a tie that broke, and a short sample often misses a real one.
summary.trap: Reading `adfuller`'s p-value or its −2.86 on a residual: 14.6% of unrelated walk pairs pass.

quiz.prose: You have two share price series and want a cointegration verdict.
quiz.question: Which order is right?

options.text: Check each leg is I(1), regress $y$ on $x$, test the residual against MacKinnon's values
Difference both, regress $\Delta y$ on $\Delta x$, test that residual
options.why: Differences are always stationary. The test must be on the levels' residual.

options.text: Regress $y$ on $x$, then read `adfuller`'s p-value on the residual
options.why: That uses the wrong critical values. 14.6% of unrelated pairs would pass.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which order tests the levels with the right critical values?
